topic: Azure Update Domain — how Azure reboots your VMs one group at a time for planned maintenance while a load balancer keeps a banking app online.
learn: How Azure reboots hosts one update domain at a time
Why the load balancer always has a healthy VM to use
Update domain versus fault domain, in one line

faq.q: What is an Azure update domain?
faq.a: A group of VMs that Azure reboots together during planned maintenance. An availability set spreads VMs across multiple update domains, so maintenance takes them down one group at a time rather than all at once.

faq.q: What's the difference between an update domain and a fault domain?
faq.a: A fault domain groups VMs by shared hardware — the same rack, power and network switch, which fail together unplanned. An update domain groups VMs by planned-maintenance timing. They protect against different kinds of interruption.

stages.title: 9,400 customers. One payments app
stages.desc: A retail banking app on Azure, 9,400 customers active right now. Transfers are clearing normally — nobody is thinking about the servers underneath.

stages.title: Two VMs behind one load balancer
stages.desc: VM1 and VM2 sit in the same availability set behind Azure Load Balancer. Every incoming transfer request is split across the two of them.

stages.title: Azure schedules host maintenance
stages.desc: Not a crash — a planned platform update on Azure's own schedule. The physical host underneath your VM needs a security patch and a reboot.

stages.title: VM1 starts installing updates
stages.desc: Azure takes update domain 0 offline first, by design. VM1 stops answering health probes and its underlying host begins the patch.

stages.title: Everyone expects the app to drop
stages.desc: Half the payment capacity is mid-reboot during a busy hour. On most architectures, this is exactly the moment the error page shows up.

stages.title: The load balancer already moved
stages.desc: The health probe on VM1 stops answering within seconds, so Azure Load Balancer drops it from the backend pool automatically.

stages.title: VM2 takes 100% of the traffic
stages.desc: Same URL, same session token, same account balance on screen. VM2 simply absorbs 100% of the transfer traffic without a blip.

stages.title: VM1 reboots and comes back
stages.desc: The physical host restarts, the VM boots back up, its health probe starts answering again — and the load balancer re-adds it immediately.

stages.title: Only now does Azure touch VM2
stages.desc: Azure explicitly waits for update domain 0 to fully recover — up to a 30-minute window — before it starts patching update domain 1 at all.

stages.title: VM1 serves while VM2 patches
stages.desc: The roles swap cleanly and automatically. The freshly patched VM1 now carries every transfer while VM2’s host reboots in its place.

stages.title: Both VMs patched. Nobody noticed
stages.desc: Two separate host reboots inside one maintenance window, and the live payments-processed counter never once dropped to zero.

stages.title: Azure Update Domain
stages.desc: That entire sequence has a name in Azure's model: an update domain is a group of VMs Azure reboots together during planned maintenance.

stages.title: One update domain at a time
stages.desc: Five update domains by default, configurable up to twenty. Azure walks through them strictly in order, waiting roughly 30 minutes after each.

stages.title: Update domain vs fault domain
stages.desc: Update domains cover the maintenance Azure deliberately schedules. Fault domains cover the hardware failure nobody ever schedules.

stages.title: Update Domain = Planned Maintenance Without Downtime
stages.desc: Spread correctly across update domains, a mandatory platform reboot becomes an invisible rolling restart instead of a customer-facing outage.

post.caption:
Azure rebooted the server running a banking app at peak hour. The payments counter never dropped to zero.

That is an update domain doing its job.

An update domain is a group of VMs in an availability set that Azure reboots together during planned platform maintenance — host OS patches, hypervisor upgrades, the work Microsoft has to do under your VM whether you like it or not.

The rule that makes it safe is boring and absolute: one update domain at a time. Azure takes UD 0 down, patches it, waits for it to come back healthy — roughly 30 minutes — and only then starts UD 1. Your VMs are spread across those domains automatically, 5 by default and up to 20 if you configure it.

Front them with Azure Load Balancer and the rest is automatic. The health probe on the rebooting VM stops answering, it leaves the backend pool, and the surviving VM absorbs the traffic. Then it swaps back. Nobody is paged. Nobody edits DNS.

The honest version, because reels tend to oversell this:
• Failover is fast, not instant. The probe has an interval and a failure threshold, so requests already in flight to the rebooting VM do fail.
• With two VMs you spend the entire maintenance window at 50% capacity. If one VM cannot carry peak load on its own, update domains just moved your outage rather than removing it. Size for N-1.
• Azure patches the host. The OS inside your VM is still yours — that is Azure Update Manager or your own tooling, not update domains.
• Session state in web server memory will log half your users out on the reboot even though the app stayed up.
• Update domains are the planned half of the story. Fault domains are the unplanned half — separate power feeds and switches for the failure nobody scheduled. One availability set gives you both.

SLA follows the design: 99.95% for two or more VMs in an availability set, against 99.9% for a single VM on premium storage.

When was the last time you actually watched what happens to your app during an Azure maintenance window?
